teaser: Half stallion, half engine, designed weeks before the war that made horses obsolete.
review_notes:
The photo shows the dark bronze against a bright window, so interior forms are hard to read; only two interactive blocks on large regions are used, and readings of forms (hoof, neck, piston) are hedged.
Conceived 1914 as a small plaster; the artist died in 1918. Enlargements were made after his death under his brothers' supervision (about 1 m in 1930-31 with Jacques Villon; about 1.5 m in 1966 with Marcel Duchamp). The Nasher cast is taken to be the 1.5 m version: please confirm size and cast date.
Duchamp-Villon studied medicine before turning to sculpture; served as a medical officer with a cavalry regiment; contracted typhoid in 1916.
His admiration in writing for the Eiffel Tower and iron engineering.

lesson.text: This horse was first worked out for a garden shed. In Puteaux, a village on the western edge of Paris, three brothers had studios around a shared yard. On Sundays painters and poets came to argue about geometry, play chess and shoot at targets. One brother, Raymond, was modeling a horse in clay.

Raymond Duchamp-Villon had trained as a doctor until illness cut his studies short, and he knew anatomy from the inside. His first sketches for the project were ordinary: a rider on a rearing animal. Then he began to strip it down. The rider went. Skin, mane and tail went.

By the summer of 1914 almost nothing horse-like was left, and something else had taken its place. Circle the bronze as this photo shows it, against the windows of the Nasher in Dallas, and name the parts if you can.

lesson.title: Animal or engine?
lesson.text: The dark shape is easier to read one piece at a time.

spots.title: The overhang
spots.text: A heavy, curved mass thrusts forward at the top, ending in a rounded knob. Many people read a lowered neck and head here. Its edges are as clean as a machine hood.

spots.title: Wheels within
spots.text: On the left, nested arcs and flat discs sit one inside the other like gears or a flywheel. Where a real horse has a muscled haunch, this one has a mechanism.

spots.title: The shaft
spots.text: A straight bar drives down through the middle to a bent, flaring form near the base that suggests a hoof. It looks like a piston rod linking engine to ground.

lesson.text: This is Cubism carried into three dimensions. Cubist painters broke objects into flat facets and showed several sides at once. Duchamp-Villon does the same with solid metal, and adds a second idea: he fuses two subjects. A leg is a connecting rod. A joint is an axle.
When war broke out in August 1914 he enlisted as a medical officer and was attached to a cavalry regiment. He kept refining the horse while on leave, after watching real ones under fire every day.

He never saw it at this size. He caught typhoid fever at the front and died in 1918, aged 41, leaving a plaster model under half a meter tall. His brothers, the painter Jacques Villon and the artist Marcel Duchamp, later had it enlarged in stages. This bronze stands about 1.5 meters (5 feet).
The Large Horse does not show what a horse looks like. It shows what a horse does: it stores energy and releases it. The forms of a machine say that more directly than fur and muscle could.
Because it portrays force more than a body, the best way in is to follow where the force goes.
Two movements run through the sculpture.

lines.label: The arch
lines.text: The outer contour rises from the left, swells over the top and curls down at the right, like a spring being wound or an animal gathering itself before a jump.

lines.label: The thrust
lines.text: From the coiled center, a diagonal shoots down to the base. This is the release: power sent from the body into the ground, the way a piston turns pressure into motion.

lesson.text: He loved engineering openly. In an essay he praised the Eiffel Tower, which many artists of his day still called ugly, as a triumph of iron and mathematics that sculptors should learn from.

There is an irony in the date. In 1914 armies still rode to war, and engine power was still measured in horses. Four years of machine guns and trucks ended that world. Duchamp-Villon's hybrid was modeled at the exact moment one kind of horsepower handed over to the other.

quiz.question: What did Duchamp-Villon study before becoming a sculptor?
quiz.explanation: He trained as a doctor until illness interrupted his studies.

quiz.question: What two things does the sculpture fuse?
quiz.explanation: Gears, shafts and pistons take the place of muscles and joints.

quiz.question: Who had the sculpture enlarged to its present size?
quiz.explanation: He left only a small plaster; Jacques Villon and Marcel Duchamp oversaw the enlargements.

quiz.question: According to the lesson, what does the sculpture show about a horse?
options: What it does: storing and releasing energy
quiz.explanation: It portrays force more than appearance.

quiz.question: Where were the brothers' studios?
options: Puteaux, on the edge of Paris
quiz.explanation: They shared a yard in Puteaux where artists met on Sundays.

facts.text: Duchamp-Villon's first sketches for the project already looked like a machine.
facts.explanation: He began with an ordinary horse and rider and stripped it down step by step.

facts.text: The artist served with a cavalry regiment during the First World War.
facts.explanation: He was a medical officer attached to the cavalry.

facts.text: He admired the Eiffel Tower and wrote in praise of it.
facts.explanation: He saw it as a triumph of iron and mathematics.
